Mr'. FOSTER. Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to call the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister to what appears to be a more definite statement regarding a matter I brought up the other day. In the morning paper I read the following:
The 'Standard's' Berlin correspondent wires: An understanding has been arrived at between Canada and Germany that negotiations for a reciprocal commercial treaty shall take place after Canada's commercial relations with United States have been regulated by the treaty now in sight. When the tariff war between Canada and Germany was terminated last year both governments agreed it was desirable to bring about a reciprocal commercial pact in the near future. At that time the Canadian and German governments concurred in the view that negotiations for a German-Canadian commercial treaty could not ensue until reciprocity had been established between Canada and United States.

Another portion of the dispatch says:
The truth is when the last tariff arrangement with the Dominion was effected in February, 1910, it was planned to renew the negotiations at no distant date for a definite treaty, but it was understood on both sides that such negotiations could only begin after Canada had regulated the tariff relations with the United States.
The assertion is also made that a definite understanding has been had between the two countries to that effect.
Mr. FIELDING, There is no understanding and there are no negotiations. I have no doubt the German government will be glad to open negotiations, but we have no such negotiations and no understanding as to when they will be taken up.

^House again in committee on Bill (No. 171) to incorporate a Grain Growers' Grain Company, Limited.-Mr. Rutan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Bill has
been considered in committee and sections 1 to 12 inclusive have been carried.
On section 13,

When this Bill was before the committee. on a previous occasion the sections up to the point you have named, Mr. Chairman went through without anybody, seemingly, paying atention to
i matter- Some questions that were asked found no answer. This is an important Bill, and somebody ought to take responsibility with reference to it. The powers asked for are very wide, and I am not sure whether the government has looked into the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have looked into it. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has gone into the matter, and I think he satisfied himself that the powers given under this Bill, though certainly very wide, are not wider than the company could have obtained by simply applying to the Under Secretary of State for letters patent of incorporation. The Senate has looked carefully into it, and, though the powers are wide, yet, for the reason I having given or for some other reason, the Senate have not thought it right to refuse the powers. And, so far as I can see no interest can be prejudiced by the measure. Certainly no representations on'the subject having been made to me. The House, no doubt, will hear from the promoter.

The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Lauriex) has stated about all that is to be said on the matter, except perhaps on one point. The other evening, when the Bill was before the committee, some objection was raised to the powers respecting banking. But the Bill as it is

now in your hands, Mr. Chairman, includes a new section which reads as follows:
18. Nothing in this Act shall he deemed to authorize the company to issue any note payable to the bearer thereof or any promissory note intended to be circulated as money or as the note of a bank, or enter into the business of banking or insurance or railway construction or operation under the provisions of the Railway Act.

The statements that the powers are not wider than those which may be got under the Companies' Act without recourse to parliament is not altogether a recommendation of this Bill. I do not know how much supervision the Finance Department exercises or wnat responsibility it takes with reference to the issuing of these charters, but certainly most extraordinary powers have been given to companies as I have noticed them going through the ' Canada Gazette.' I think it is an axiom that will be pretty well assented to that the title of a Bill ought to be an indication of the powers granted under it, so that one who reads the title may thereby understand generally what the Bill is intended to do. Now the title of this Bill is ' An Act to Incorporate the Grain Growers' Grain Company.' But when you look at the Bill you find that it goes away beyond grain, and by what connection or process of logic I do not know. Here is section 13:
The objects or purposes of the company shall be to produce, manufacture, import, export, buy, sell, deal in and deal with all cereals

Now, that is grain, and comes fairly within the limts of the title. It goes on:
-fruit, vegetable, animal, or other products of the farm

That does not go very tar away, for it all comes from the farm and there is a logical connection.
-all products or by-products thereof

That is logical also.
-and all machinery, implements, goods, wares and merchandise whioh may be used in the production and _ manufacture of products of the farm,

That also has a connection with the purposes of the Bill.
-and all articles, substances and things which may be utilized in the said production or in the maintenance, cultivation, improvement and development of farms.
That seems to me to go almost as wide as the horizon. It would enable them to become a plough manufacturing company or a harvester company, or a company for the production of anything that may be used on the farm. It will make them almost universally a manufacturing company. A man is not (in the Northwest) likely to go out to work without a shirt on his back, and it might be logically taken from these powers that if a shirt was necessary to a man working the company would have a perfect right to go into the manufacturing of shirts, to clothe farmers when they work, and the same with shoes caps and other articles of wear. It goes on:
And, without restricting the generality of the foregoing expressions

That is a pretty rich phrase. After taking in the universe, you say you do not want to be restricted because there may be other universes that you may wish to conquer. There may be abstruse problems relating to the farms of the future, such as the manufacture of sunlight, or the using of the vital forces

Sunbeams from cucumbers.
' Mr. FOSTER. Oh, if they wanted to manufacture sunbeams they would annex the Premier (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and their factory would be complete.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I wish you would appreciate that.

I do.
And, without restricting the generality of the foregoing expressions, to carry on the business of a farmer in all its branches.
Now, section 14 goes on. And, really, has the Prime Minister looked into this at all?
For the objects and purposes set forth in section 13 of this Act, the company may:
(a.) Manufacture, buy, sell, deal in and deal with timber

It may become a timber company.
-lumber,

It may become a lumber company.
-hardware,


It may become a general hardware company.
-bricks, stone, tiles, wood products of all kinds, building materials of every description, and all kinds of merchandise and supplies.
It may become a haberdashery, anything, almost, in the wide world in the way of merchandise and supplies. It goes on:
(b.) Manufacture, develop, transmit, distribute and use pneumatic, hydraulic, electric or other power or force for any purpose for which the same may be used

Now there would be a logical connection if it were allowed to engage in the manufacture of these things as an agent or instrument of the farm; but it is only restricted by the phrase ' for the objects and purposes set forth in section 13.' In fact,

it does not only not restrict, but it carries away from it any possible restriction.

for any purpose for which the same may be used

They may become an electric lighting company to supply electric light for a town; they may become a hydraulic company, a pneumatic company, and may lay tubes for the transmission of merchandise all through the country, not for the sake of spouting grain or other products of the farm, but 'for any purpose whatsoever.'
-and manufacture, buy, sell and deal in all machinery, implements and material necessary for the manufacture, development, transmission and distribution of pneumatic, hydraulic, electric or other force: Provided, however, that any distribution or transmission of power or force beyond the lands of the company shall be subject to local and municipal regulations in that behalf.
(c.) Purchase, acquire, develop, operate, hold, dispose of or otherwise turn to account timber lands, timber licenses, coal lands, quarries, water-powers and other lands for the purposes of the company;
(d.) Subscribe for, purchase or otherwise acquire and hold, sell or otherwise dispose of the shares, bonds, debentures or other securities of any bank, or of any printing or publishing company, but in the case of a bank, to no greater extent than one-fourth of the capital stock of such bank.
That is a strange power to give to a grain company.
(e.) Purchase or otherwise acquire, build, operate and charter ships, barges, vessels or other means of transporting passengers and cargo by water.
That clause is not limited to the purposes of this company, it is widened until there is no restriction upon it at all. They may become a shipbuilding or ship running company for the transportation of passengers and freight other than those necessary for their own operation.
(f.) Enter into any arrangement with any authorities, municipal, local or otherwise, that may seem conducive to the company's objects, or any of them

May seem conducive to themselves.
-and obtain from any such authority any rights, privileges and concessions which the company may think it desirable to obtain and carry out, exercise and comply with any such arrangements, rights, privileges and concessions.
(g.) Acquire or undertake the whole or any part of the business, property and liabilities of any person or company carrying on any business which the company is authorized to carry on, or possessed of property suitable for the purposes of the company.
The company is authorized practically to carry on every business; they are not only authorized to carry on any business, but to enter into financial arrangements Mr. FOSTER
for the sake of the company, into buying, selling and the like of that."
(h.) Apply for, purchase or otherwise acquire, any patents, licenses, concessions and the like, conferring any exclusive or non-exclusive, or limited rights to use, or any secret or other information as to any invention which may seem capable of being used for any of the purposes of the company-*-
That is for any purpose whatsoever.
-or the acquisition of which may seem calculated directly or indirectly to benefit the company, and use, exercise, develop or grant licenses in respect of, or otherwise turn to account, the property, rights or information so acquired.
It seems to me that is wide enough to send them up to the Yukon and get gold concessions.
(i.) Construct, improve, maintain, work, manage, carry out or control any roads, ways, tramways, branches or sidings on lands owned or controlled by the company,

Not only gives them the right to own any kind of lands, any kind of concessions, but it gives them every particular privilege.
-bridges, reservoirs, water courses, wharfs, manufactures, warehouses, elevators, electric works, shops, stores, office buildings and other works and conveniences, and contribute to, subsidize or otherwise assist or take part in, the construction, improvement, maintenance, working, management, carrying out or control thereof.
Pretty wide power that is.
That is the standard called for in the Ontario Act.

What does my hon. friend think about the wideness of the powers? Can he imagine anything that they cannot do?
(j.) Lend money to customers and others having dealings with the company

That is, they may lend not simply to their own people, they are authorized to lend money generally, no restrictions to whom they may lend.
That clause has been amended in the committee.

-and guarantee the performance of contracts by any such persons; notwithstanding the provisions of section 167 of the Company's Act.
(k) Draw, make, accept, endorse, discount, execute and issue promissory notes, bills of exchange, bills of lading, warrants and other negotiable or transferable instruments.
There is no limit to it.
(1.) Sell or dispose of the undertaking of the company, or any part thereof, for such consideration as the company may think fit, and in particular, for shares, debentures or

securities of any other company having objects altogether or in part similar to those of the company.
How large a part? A very infinitesmal part, I suppose.
(m.) To do all or any of the above things as principals, agents, contractors, trustees or otherwise, and either alone or in conjunction with others.
(n.) To do all such other things as are incidental or conducive to the attainment of the objects or purposes of the company.
It struck me as I read that over that, although such things may have passed this parliament, it is an exceedingly wide franchise to give to a grain growers' company or any other company. I suppose some good-hearted individuals will be ready to say that I oppose this Bill because it belongs to the grain growers, that they are 'introducing it. I give every privilege to any person to make that assertion who wishes. I am .used to that kind of thing, and it doesn't bother me a bit. I do not go as far as the Minister of Finance went the other day, when he intimated that almost he wouid let a poor thing go through rather than have somebody say that he didn't like to do a thing for a certain class of people. I think that legislation like this is extremely dangerous. Time was in this House when no legislation like that could possibly go through, and that not very long ago. But the government must take the responsibility. Mine is but a voice in the wilderness, but it will be raised for a moment to direct the attention of the treasury board, if they take any interest in these things, to the almighty powers that are being given to this company.

I quite agree with the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in his remarks as to the wideness of the powers granted by this charter. When the Bill was last before the committee I drew attention to the same feature, and was then assured by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) that the same powers would have been granted automatically if the company had applied under the Companies' Act. To that assurance there is now added a further assurance to the same effect by the Prime Minister. Consequently, while I cannot but sanction many of the remarks by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) as to the danger of such almost indiscriminately wide powers passing this House, still I must again take the point that, under the assurance 'to which I have referred, this is not the stage at which to take the objection. If this company, merely by application under the Companies' Act, could secure all the powers granted in this Bill, surely I would not be justified in saying
to them:	If you come openly before parliament individually and make application we will shut you out of powers that you might have got automatically under the Act that we have ourselves passed. Surely such a position on the part of parliament would be inconsistent and unreasonable. If there are dangers in the general granting of such utterly limitless powers as this Bill provides, then the place to remedy that condition, and to curtail the powers is in the Companies' Act itself.
Does the hon. gentleman think that if they have all these powers they should have them under the name of the Grain Growers' Grain Company?

I was coming to that point. I have said nothing that can be urged as an argument in favour of the title of the Bill, in fact to my mind the gravest point of danger in all this legislation is in chartering a company with indiscriminately wide powers under a distinctive name. In that way the public is liable to be deceived. It may tax the ingenuity of the promoter of the Bill, it may even tax the still greater ingenuity of the fathers of the Bill, to provide a name that can be called distinctive and at the same time can be called a safe one for the proposed company to assume, but an attempt should be made to make such name better conform to the general character of the charter. It seems to me that the word * grain ' when it occurs the second time in the title of the company, might very well be omitted in favour of something more general; the grain feature of the purposes of the company is surely well enough to emphasize in the expression 'Grain Growers.' So if the difficulty as to name could be met it seems to me that parliament would not be justified in raising further objection to the Bill, on the general ground at least.
The applicants for this charter are just as much entitled to secure it as any other applicants; consequently if parliament- and I believe the assurances we have are correct, that a reference to the ' Canada Gazette ' will show that as wide powers are granted under the Companies' Act-if parliament by its Act confers ion individuals the right to go to our Department .of State and secure just as wide powers as these, then, we have no justification for stepping in and in an individual case refusing the powers asked. The only objection that I take is as to the title. Under that title I fear shares will be purchased with an assurance as to the purpose's of the company that really is a false one. The point is doubly important when we remember that heretofore in Manitoba a company under the very same name has been operating, and that company is much

more restricted in its powers than this company will be.
Is my hon. friend sure of that? The promoter of the Bill tells me that the powers are wider than these.
How can you make them wider?

They could be made wider. In this Bill the powers given by section 14, must be exercised solely for the purpose of carrying out the objects and purposes set forth in section 13. There is a limitation. I have only the word of my hon. friend who is in charge of the Bill as to the powers granted by the Manitoba charter being wider, and he tells me they are wider. I have not seen the Manitoba charter.

The Minister of Public Works says that one clause of the charter provides that the powers therein granted shall only be utilized in so far as they serve the general purpose of the company, and argues that that is a restriction. If the general purposes of the company are utterly unlimited, how is that a restriction?
They are not unlimited under section 13.

My reason for saying that the Manitoba powers are not as wide is that I have myself, as solicitor, applied to the Provincial Secretary's Department at Winnipeg, where the charter of the original company would be granted, and I know that if the application made anything like so large a demand on the generosity of that department, the powers asked would be very seriously curtailed before the charter was issued. I have not examined this particular charter, but I would be surprised if the powers under which they have been operating are as wide as those contained in this Bill. The company in Manitoba has done business for many years, and the scope of its business has been limited to such pursuits as should be contemplated under the old title. It is evidently the intention of the company to widen the scope of its operations, as I gather from other sources than the Bill. If that is the intention, the title of the Bill should be altered. I do not think that is raising an insuperable objection, and I have no intention of raising such an objection. My objection is one that could, within reason be overcome, and if it is overcome any opposition, if it may be called opposition, that I have raised to the Bill would be at once withdrawn.

I cannot see the force of the objection raised; by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, to this company being incorporated under the name of the Grain Growers Grain Company, Limited, Mr. MEIGHEN.
for the obvious reason he mentioned, that the company has been doing business in Manitoba, under a joint stock company charter, and I believe in Alberta, under a foreign company's license, for almost five years. I am not positive that they have been doing any business in Saskatchewan, but they have acquired certain assets in Alberta, and certain large assets in Manitoba. To my mind it would be manifestly unfair for parliament to change the name of the company after it has been doing business with that name for five years.
A name exactly similar?

Yes. The statement made by the Minister of Public Works with respect to the powers granted to this company by the government of Manitoba being as wide as the powers contained in this Bill is, to my mind, perfectly correct.
In what year was that charter granted?

I have here what purports to be a copy of the letters patent granted by the Provincial Secretary of Manitoba, and dated July 20, 1906, almost five years ago. It is a copy of the charter of the Grain Growers' Grain Company, Limited, which is the same name as we are asked to grant, under the proposed Act of incorporation. I beg to call attention to some of the powers granted in the charter of the Grain Growers' Grain Company, Limited-the same name exactly-and it will be seen that these powers are exactly the same as asked for in this Bill. They have power to buy, handle, and deal in all kinds of grain and seed, both as owners and agents; power to manufacture, buy, handle, and deal in agricultural implements and machinery, coal, coal oil, gasoline, and a large list of other commodities; power to acquire by purchase, lease or otherwise, with the consent of the owners, mines, mining lands, minerals, of all kinds; power to acquire by purchase, lease, or otherwise, witlj the consent of the owners, water-powers, water-power rights and privileges; and to develop for the purposes of the company or lease, or sell, electrical, steam, pneumatic gas, hot-air; and all descriptions of power. There is a clause here permitting them to manufacture bicycles and automobiles which one would not expect the farmers of Canada to deal in. The original letters patent contain everything contained in the purposed Bill, and why should parliament curtail the powers they have for five years enjoyed under a provincial charter? Although the powers asked for are wide, they are properly limited by section 18 prohibiting them from building railroads, which the hon. member for Prince Albert asks to add to the Bill. There is no reason why the Bill should not go through with that amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If this were purely an abstract question I would be disposed to agree very generally with my hon. friend from North Toronto. The wide powers asked for by this company have shocked his Conservative principles, and I tell him frankly that they shock my Liberal principles, or rather the principles I learned in the school I was brought up in. But my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) must observe that the ideas in which he and I have been brought up have been very much enlarged of late years. When first the creation of corporations became somewhat general, parliament was very chary in the granting of charters, and the powers given were severely scrutinized, and restricted practically to the special object for which incorporation was sought. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) knows that in his experience, as in mine, there has been an everincreasing tendency to widen these powers until now we give to companies, as he has said, a sort of omnibus charter to do any kind of business at all. When you look into the rationale of the thing, I do not think there can be any danger in granting these wide powers except the possible danger of deceiving the public.
That is a very great danger.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is. But the public is educated to the change, and it is realized now that if you authorize a grain company the title would not at all deceive those who deal with that company into the belief that its powers would be restricted to operations in grain. There would be no deception of the public because it is now generally known that there are wider powers granted than the title would indicate. This company has been granted already powers by the legislature of Manitoba, and we are now asked to confirm these powers, but with certain restrictions added. I understand that in the western states you can file your application to build a railway at the Capitol and some officer corresponding to our Secretary of State looks into the matter, and the charter is granted as a matter of course.
Without any guarantees?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So I am told. I understand that some such powers were sought by this Bill, but that is further than I would go, and that, I think, parliament should go. The granting of such wide powers may be contrary to the views of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster), and, perhaps, contrary to my own views, but the western farmers and the western people generally, are disposed to seek corporate powers which we would never think of asking for in the east. It may be that we will have to advance to the same views as they have. Though this granting of wide powers in 270	m
charters has been going on for some time, it has not come to my notice that it has produced any ill results.
I admit there is something in what my right hon. friend has said, although I do not admire his dialectics in this respect. He says that I am a Conservative and that he used to be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Oh, no, I
never said that.

Well, there is more than a modicum of truth in that, if history informs us correctly, but I think that even he is not quite liberal enough to swallow so extensive a programme with so modest a name. My chief objection is the possible danger of deception because of the wide divergence between the name of the company and what it may do. There are two forces in the world: one Liberal, and the other Conservative, and if you go through the world's history it is difficult to award the palm to either as being the most beneficial to the race.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not difficult for me.	. ,

It would be if my right hon. friend studied it a bit. The maddish projects of Liberalism have been nipped in the bud by the quantum of Conservatism which has always existed in the world, and which I hope always will. On the other hand, Conservatism advances from year to year, because changed conditions necessitate a widening process in the application of old principles of Conservatism. I hope the day will never come when there will not be these two forces in the world, the one tending to restrict mad, headlong haste, and the other tending to stretch out and broaden that which would otherwise be cribbed, Cabined and confined.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And in the
interests of the people, progress and advancement must come.

These, two forces have their cycles; one comes down and [DOT] the other goes up, and they keep their balance pretty well, and so my right hon. friend had better prepare for the balance which will swing the other way pretty soon. I sound the note * of warning that this Bill represents Liberalism gone too far. They cannot carry on all these projects without getting money, and they appeal for money under the distinctive guise of a grain company and under that distinctive badge ninety-nine men out of a hundred will subscribe to it because of its purpose in that respect. There is great danger that under a certain guise a company could carry on almost every kind of operation under the sun. To show my right hon. friend just what took place, I may say that in my



time, and it was not so very long ago, a company was restricted to the simple purpose indicated by its name, and even subsidiary operations were not allowed, because they were not considered a legitimate part of that purpose. That idea has completely passed away. Such has been the extension of work in the world that the next step was to allow not only the prime object of the company, but what might be subsidiary thereto, and what might be necessary for its operation. That was a legitimate and fair extension, and I am willing to go as far as that principle can extend. But I think it is dangerous to put a big company, which acts as a grain company, into the business of mining, stock-buying and all that sort of thing. I think that, goes beyond where we ought to go, and I take exception, mildly but still firmly, to the idea that because some other legislature has granted extraordinary rights and powers, therefore we should, do it. I am sorry the Finance Minister is not here, because I would like to inquire of him whether there is any supervision at all over these companies who are getting charters without coming to parliament, or any revision of the powers asked for by them. I am loth to take the statement of the Prime Minister, and of the Minister of Public Works that company charters have been granitoid equally wide with this. Some very wide opes, I know, have been granted, but I think it would trouble them to find one as wide as this is. I would like to know whether the government applies any supervising machinery at all to keep within bounds the companies that ask for charters without coming to this House. Does the Companies' Act require that a return should be made to the government of the operation of these companies?
Only as to loan companies, I think.
I think it is well worth consideration whether every one of these companies should not be required to make a return to the government.
There is a Bill before the House this session making provision for that. I do not think that under the Bill the companies are bound to supply the returns, but they may be called for.

I am stating my general objection to the granting of these wide powers in this Bill. If it is allowed to pass, the government will have to take the responsibility, and it will not be in the power of the First Minister, or of the Minister of Finance, to say that I am equally responsible, because f did not object to the Bill when it. went through parliament.

My hon. friend has called attention to a difficulty that might Mr. FOSTER.	.
arise by reason of the name. I may say that that is the only objection I saw to the Bill; but, on considering the matter, I do not see that we could choose a name for the company if my hon. friend in charge of the Bill was not willing to have the name changed. I do not see why we should refuse these powers, which are substantially the same as were contained in the charter granted by the Manitoba legislature, and they are no wider than the powers that might, properly be given by letters patent issued by the Secretary of State.
Does my hon. friend know that, or is that a general statement?

I know that, because when I was Attorney General in the government of New Brunswick, I took objection for some time to the granting of wide powers, and my attention was called to the powers granted for years by the Dominion government, and also by other provinces. The government of Ontario is the chief sinner in this respect, if there is any sin about it.
It used to be, I know.

The province of Ontario first gave these bioad powers. My hon. friend made a very pleasant speech in regard to the Prime Minister and his own Conservatism. I presume that if my hon. friend saw that the present government of Ontario had recognized and granted a license to a company incorporated by the parliament of Great Britain conferring upon it practically the same powers as are contained in this Bill, he would say that was Conservatism enough.
I do not take my Conservatism from anybody.

Let me call attention to a license which has been granted by the government of Ontario, as late as the 15th of April of the present year, to the Alberta Land Company, to do business in the province of Ontario. It is incorporated, says the notice published in the ' Ontario Gazette,' by the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain, and it is given the power first, to acquire lands; secondly, to improve the lands; thirdly, to stock the same; to go into the buying of all kinds of stock, cattle, sheep and produce; to buy, manufacture, sell and deal in all kinds of goods, chattels, merchandise and effects; to carry on the business of farmers, graziers, meat and fruit preservers, planters, miners, metallurgists, quarry-owners, brick makers, builders, contractors for the construction of works, both public and private, merchants, importers and exporters, printers, publishers, ship-builders shipowners brokers and any other businesses which may seem calculated, directly or indirectly, to develop the company's property or business; to search or prospect,

excavate, quarry, dredge for ores, and to extract, reduce and treat the same by any process whatsoever; to pay for any property or business in shares "or debentures; to sell, lease, license, mortgage, turn to account or otherwise dispose of any of the property, concessions, rights or privileges of the company; to exercise within the province of Ontario all such powers under the laws of Ontario. There you find a company incorporated under the name of a land company, and yet given the power to engage in mining, quarrying, buying and selling merchandise of all kinds, owning ships and doing a large business, which could in no way be associated by the investor with the business of carrying on a land company.
The hon. gentleman will not say that it is at all as wide as this Bill.

Substantially so, because if you take this Bill you will find that after all section 13 is the one which sets out the objects of the company. These are limited to manufacturing and dealing in ceTeals, fruit, vegetable, animal or other products of the farm, all products or by-products thereof, and all machinery, implements, goods, wares and merchandise which may be used in the production and manufacture ' of products of the farm, and all articles, substances and things which may be utilized in the said production or in the maintenance, cultivation, improvement and development of farms. All these are pTetty closely connected with the foregoing business of farming. Then, ' without restricting the generality of the expressions, to carry-on the business of farming in all its branches.' When we come to 'section 14, you will see a limitation. It may not be very perfect, but still it is a limitation.
' For the objects and purposes set forth in section 13 of the Act, the company may do certain things.' It seems to me that in the bona fide carrying out of the powers contained in section 14, the directors must always have in mind the purposes and objects set forth in section 13. They may build electric railways through their properties, develop electricity to supply their farms with motive power, buy steamers for the purpose of carrying grain produced by their operations, to the different markets of the world, and do all these things connected with the carrying out of the object mentioned in section 13.
Is the hon. gentleman taking hi's politics from the province of Ontario now?
I did not know there were any politics in this. I am surprised at the suggestion of my hon. friend.

It 'seems to me that one of the objections is that this is 270i	-
a very small name for a large company. I give this suggestion to the promoter. Call it the almighty powers of the grain growers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear. There is something in that.
I would suggest that there ought to be one extension of the powers to be given this company. It ought to have the power to manufacture M. P.s of the Liberal persuasion.
What is the reason this company has made application to this House for a charter? Why did it not apply for letters patent?
The only reason is that they were taking over a growing concern, the Grain Growers' Company, and assuming all its liabilities, and took this method of getting a charter.

The only reason why the company did not ask for a charter from the Secretary of State is because, when a charter is granted by the Secretary of State, the company is bound to make returns to the provincial government. The right hon. gentleman is probably aware that there is a Bill before a special committee for weeks, and a great deal of care has been taken to secure such returns as will give to the shareholders in these companies the fullest information; but by getting the charter asked for here they will not be under the obligation of disclosing their proceedings.
On section 14,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The section (b) has been amended to read as follows:
(b) manufacture, develop, transmit, distribute and use pneumatic, hydraulic, electric or other power or force for any purpose for which the same may be used, and manufacture, buy, sell and deal in all machinery, implements and material necessary for the manufacture, development, transmission and distribution of pneumatic, hydraulic, electric or other power or force: Provided, however, that any distribution or transmission of power or force beyond the lands of the company shall be subject to section 247 of the Railway Act and so far as applicable to the ^Electricity Inspection Act of 1907, and the 'local and municipal regulations in that behalf.

In all of these companies we put in a clause that they cannot do anything of that kind without the consent of the municipality by Iby-law. But the words here ' shall be subject to local and municipal regulations ' are not as strong as permission expressed by by-law.
In the Railway Committee, Bills for the incorporation of railway companies are always safeguarded with provisions to the effect mentioned by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt).
The clerk of the 'committee says that this is the standard clause taken from the other Bills.

There is power here not only to manufacture, but also to distribute electrical energy. That distribution would involve the right to distribute in the usual way by wires and poles. Yet there is no provision as to the assent of the municipality for entering or crossing highways or public places. These safeguards have been put in Bills in the Railway Committee. And, unless section 247 of the Railway Act covers the regulation of rates to be charged for power, there is no provision to limit through the Board of Railway Commissioners the rates to be charged by the company, for electrical energy. And the same in regard to telegraph and telephones -there is no regulation either of rates nor is there any safeguard of the rights of municipalities.
These precautions are provided in other charters. There was one the other day that the Finance Minister sent back to get this clause put in. And this one should be treated the same as the others.
So it is. The committee has that in.
I do not so understand it. Section 247 of the Railway Act does not cover it-certainly does not cover the question of charges.
It was the clerk of the committee who had this prepared, and he said it was a standard clause put in the other Bills.

I think the objection is well taken by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell). There does not seem to be any control over this company as to entering the bounds of municipalities, nor is there any safeguard as to the rates to be charged. There is no reason why the safeguards put in other Bills should not be put in this.

Does not the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) think that the clause subject to" local and municipal regulations in that behalf would prevent the company from distributing power within any municipality unless it got the authority of a by-law?

I have been in the Railway Committee and have seen the committee jump like a panther on a clause in a Bill which did not provide in the most explicit way for the guarding of municipal rights. That safeguarding of municipal rights, so far as my _ experience goes, has been expressed in this way. Then, again, it does not say anything as to rates. Here Mr. MACDONELL.
is a company which is going to carry on telephones and telegraphs and the transmission of intelligence, and there is absolutely no control over its rates. We must be consistent. No matter for whom the Bill is we must have these safeguards put in.

If the purpose of the amendment is to bring in the whole of section 247 of the Railway Act, then, both hon. gentlemen are partly right. I have the section before me, and it proposes that the consent of the municipality must first be obtained. But, unfortunately for the powers of municipalities this section provides that, if the consent is not given, the Board of Railway Commissioners may override a municipality and grant the power desired. Personally, I do not think that a municipality ought to be shorn of its power over its highways. I think they are the best judges in this _ matter. The section is a very long one, with many subsections, but I will read the parts that apply :
When any company is empowered by special Act of the parliament of Canada to construct, operate and maintain, lines of telegraph, or telephone or for the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity, the company may, with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over any highway, square or other public place, enter thereon for the purpose of exercising the said powers, and, as often as the company thinks proper, may break up and open any highway, square or other public place, subject, however, in the following provisions:
It then proceeds to lay down a lot of rules with regard to wires, and poles, supervision by an officer of a municipal council, and so on, until we come to subsection (g) **
Whenever any city, town or incorporated village is desirous of having lines of telegraph, or telephone, or lines for the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity, placed under ground, the board may,

That is the Board of Railway Commissioners :	.
-may, on the application of such city, town or incorporated village, and on such terms and conditions as the board may prescribe, require the company to thus place its lines or wires under ground, and abrogate the right given by this section, or by the special Act, to carry lines on poles, in such city, town or incorporated village.
That is a section for the benefit of municipalities. Where the company does not serve the municipality they can apply to the board. Then the converse is provided:
If the company cannot obtain such consent from such municipal council or other authority, the company may apply to the board for leave to exercise such powers, and upon such

application shall submit to the board a plan of such highway, square, or other publio place, showing the proposed location of such lines, wires and poles.
Then it goes on that the board may, notwithstanding the refusal to consent of the municipality, allow the matter to be so done:
How about the regulation of rates?

That is under another section. Then, at the end of the section it is provided:
Nothing contained in this section shall be deemed to authorize the company to exercise the powers therein mentioned for the purpose of selling or distributing light, heat, power or electricity in cities, towns or villages, without the company having first obtained consent therefore by a by-law of the municipality.
There is another quasi-protection so far as cities, towns and villages are concerned, but not to all municipalities. There are many other municipalities whose roads are valuable to them, municipalities in an embryo state, but growing. I think that all municipalities ought to be protected, whether in their infancy or in an advanced state of growth. But, because of the want of satisfactory provisions, or to meet some complication, we do sometimes insert a general clause providing that these things are only to be done by consent of the municipality expressed by by-law. We also make a distinct provision that rates and charges are to be subject to the control of the Railway Commission. I think we ought to put that clearly in this Bill. I do not offer an amendment at this stage, but I would suggest that the amendment before the Chair be so worded that the consent of the municipalities be obtained, and that the rates be subject to the control of some authority.

How would it do to put in a clause like this:
Provided, however, that in no case shall the company place any poles in or upon any highway, or stretch any wires along such highway or over any public square or park without the consent of the municipal council in which the same is situated.
That would still send it to the board for regulation.
But it does not meet the question of rates.
But it makes it subject to the local municipal regulations. They would make a condition of having reasonable rates before they would give consent.
I agree with the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) that the two standard clauses usually put in Bills should be put in this Bill.

There are two regular clauses spoken of as the standard clauses. One is in regard to the consent of the municipality to the company stringing its wires, or erecting poles upon, or across any highway, or public place; then there is another clause with regard to rates. I think these clauses should be put in, and for that purpose I would suggest that this subsection (b) be allowed to stand.
Let us report progress, and have these two standard clauses drawn up.

I think that is wise. If anybody ought to be tender about the rights of municipalities and reasonable rates it is the grain growers. I do not see why there should be any objection to inserting these two standard clauses.

I see no objection to letting the section stand over for the purpose of Inserting these clauses. But we can go on with the rest of the Bill,
On subsection (d),
, Mr. FOSTER. What is the purpose of this clause:
Subscribe for, purchase or otherwise acquire, and hold, sell or otherwise dispose of, the shares, bonds, debentures, or other securities of any bank, or of any printing or publishing company.
What does the Grain Company propose in that?

This company owns a publication called the 'Grain Growers' Guide,' that is a part of their business.
, Mr. FOSTER. But that is their own paper. Here they have authority to take over other papers, it gives them authority to buy up every newspaper in the northwest.
, Mr. RUTAN. They have the same right as other people with regard to that.
It is funny that a Grain .Company is becoming a great publishing company.

It seems to me an improper thing to give an ostensible grain company power to embark in the banking business by allowing them to purchase shares, or stocks in a bank to the extent of one-fourth of their capital. They can use the bank for the purpose of exploiting funds, for the purpose of dealing in grain; and they have an additional power of being able to build up a press and publish papers which could be used for the purpose of advancing or depressing prices. This company are also dealers in, and buyers of grain. It seems to me a most unusual thing to give a company power to do all these things under one corporation. They

,can exploit the funds of a bank, and deal in grain, and by their press they can exploit public opinion for the purpose of raising or depressing markets.
On subsection (e),
There should be the same clause with regard to the regulation of rates that I spoke of in regard to subsection (c).
You do not regulate rates on vessels. No other vessels have their rates regulated.

I think where railway companies are given charters, as they are in the Railway Committee from day to day, and where these companies have also navigation powers, the Railway Board has the power to regulate the rates.
I think my hon. friend is in error as to that. Where a subsidy is granted the government may make some provision, not otherwise.
Does the Minister of Public Works say that the present Railway Commission has not a right to regulate rates for a railway which does business by land and by water?

I understand we have no power to regulate rates on the steamers. When subsidies are granted the government make certain provisions, but I do not think the Railway Commission has any power to regulate steamship rates.

That is a rather important point because the purpose of the Railway Commission to regulate the rates might be entirely set at nought, provided you had a railway company which also ran ships, if there was no power to regulate the water passage.
That would not apply to this company because they do not build railways.
They are getting powers here to carry passengers.
There is a clause that nothing herein contained shall give them power to build railways. They are expressly barred from building railways.

Section 333 of the Railway Act is important in view of what has been said toy the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). In this section the word 'company' of course means a railway company. The section reads:
Subsection 3. If the company owns, charters, uses, maintains or works, or is a party to any arrangement for using, maintaining or working vessels for carrying traffic, by sea or inland water, between any places or ports in Canada, and if any such vessel carries Mr. MACDONELL.
traffic between a port in Canada reached by such company and a port in Canada reached by the railway of another company, the vessel and the railway of either company shall be deemed to constitute a continuous route in Canada within the meaning of this section.
Thus the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is right, and the minute you allow this company to do business in water carriage you should put them under the control of the Railway Commission.
Subsection (e) allowed to stand.
On subsection (g), power to acquire other companies,
That is a very wide section. Is not the minister afraid of a combination? This might lead to a huge monopoly.
That is the usual clause.

If that is the general Act it ought to be amended. The danger is the very simplicity and wide nature of the language. We are authorizing this company to do everything except practise medicine and law, and now we are saying that in all these lines of business they may touy up everybody in opposition to them.

That Is what is always done in letters patent; the company being incorporated may acquire the business and undertaking of any company authorized to carry on a similar business. I venture to say that the same powers will be found in the charter of incorporation of the Canada Cement Company. It is the usual clause in commercial or industrial companies.
I do not think we should pass the section without further consideration. I douJbt if the Grain Growers' Company wish to be made into a huge monopoly like that.
If they wanted to buy out a flour mill would it be any more harm than for them to build a new mill?

Yes. Suppose you have only two companies operating in a certain way and have competition between them, then the minister's question answers itself; you allow one company to buy out the other, and you immediately lose all competition and have a monopoly.
It is not necessary to buy them out in order to have no competition, so far as price is concerned.

My point is that if a person is a strong opponent to monopolies, he should oppose this section because it has a decidedly monopolistic tendency. If they have capital enough they can buy out every single business, and you would have

most certainly a most complete monopoly. It would not be possible to frame a more monopolistic clause. I leave it to my hon. friend for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) if that is not so.	.

I think the clause is too wide, and that all similar clauses in all these Bills are too wide, but I think we should commence the reform by revising the Companies Act. Take all these mergers that have been formed in the last few years, and they just last until some one else has time to build a factory. I do not believe there is any particular danger in this clause, but I do think, generally speaking, that all such clauses are wrong from a legislative standpoint.

When, earlier in the session, I called attention to a similar clause in the McClary Manufacturing Company's Bill, promoted by my hon. friend (Mr. Beattie), my remarks got no sympathy from either side of the House.
Were I here you would have mine.
The McClary Bill authorized the company to purchase the stock of any other company which manufactures any goods similar to those manufactured, by the McClary Company.
There is a vast distinction between that provision, and the provisions of this Bill. That company was engaged in manufacturing stoves, and it was authorized to acquire any company similarly engaged.
A monopoly in stoves would be hurtful.

This Bill authorizes the grain growers to do everything except build railways or practise law or medicine. You allow this company to buy up everything that is in its road, and you create an evil tenfold greater than that which the Minister of Public Works says existed in the McClary case.
The House did not think there was anything wrong in the McClary case.
Is the minister so modest that he will recede from his opinion, and now say that what is tenfold worse than the McClary case, is right?

The very day this Bill passed the Private Bills Committee, the McClary Company was given the right to purchase an interest in every retail business throughout the country, and no objection was raised. That is much more dangerous than any provision of this Bill. The McClary Company are doing business with retail merchants throughout the whole
country, and if they get into the debt of the McClary Manufacturing Company they, the company, can say: 'We must protect ourselves, and we will insist on you giving us an interest in your business,' a power which tends to enable them to monopolize the retail business throughout the country.
And under this Bill the grain growers can buy up a retailer, or a wholesaler, or any one else that comes in their road.

This is not an opportune time to say that the farmers, who are the Grain Growers Company, should not be given the same privilege as is given _ to others. I do not see why a manufacturing company should be allowed this power, and why it should be refused to farmers.

This Bill says that they are going to do everything else except farming. They are going to deal in real estate, and have a printing house, and run banks. I am as good a friend^of the farmer as is the hon. gentleman, or anybody else, but when a farmer ceases to be a farmer, and is not satisfied with growing grain and dealing in grain, but wants to do everything else except farming, then he has no right to come here and plead for sympathy because he is a farmer. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Rutan), comes here and pleads, that under the name of a. farmers association they can rope people in just as in the case of the Farmers' Bank. When farmers are acting as farmers they deserve our sympathy, and encouragement, and support, but when they cease to be farmers they should go on the same plane as other people.

The clause in the McClary Bill makes provision as to the conditions under which the company may do these thing3, such as authorization by by-law, and a meeting of directors, and so on. These appear to be salutary conditions.
The McClary Bill allows the directors to do it, and in this case the shareholders have to do it.
If the provisions of the Bill are not satisfactory in that respect, they can he made so.
I wish the hon. member for Essex would keep that in mind as we go through the clauses of the Bill.

It is all very well to talk about creating a monopoly, but there is another view which may be taken. The apparent object of this Bill is that the farmers desire to cut out -the middlemen. For instance, instead of getting their lumber from a sawmill they may manufacture it themselves, and in like manner they take power to manufacture agricul-

tural implements, and such necessaries which, under the present conditions, they have to purchase from other concerns. No doubt if this association is a success every farmer will become a member of it, and if they find a sawmill in a small town in the west where there is only room for one sawmill, they can buy that mill out by agreement with the owner rather than start another mill which would be ruinous to both. If it is a necessity for one to sell, and the other to purchase there can be no harm in giving this company power to purchase.

Does not the hon. gentleman see that the legitimate inference to be drawn from his argument is pure socialism? Is that the object of the hon. gentleman, or diversity of trade and occupation in the country?

The farmers in the west not only grow grain, but afterwards have to dispose of it. The experience of the western farmers for a good many years has been that in disposing of their crop, more especially their wheat, to the ordinary purchasers of grain, they were not able to get the full value of the grain when it left their hands owing to combinations among the purchasers or middlemen. The farmers organized themselves into this Grain Growers' Grain Company, and for twro or three years past they have been handling the grain to a large extent through this company, with the result that they have been able, owing to the fact that this association has about 30,000 members in the three prairie provinces, to get nearer to the full value of their crops than they ever did before. The company was in a position to handle a large enough proportion of the crop to prevent other buyers organizing and putting down the price as formerly. The farmers have learned, by their experience in organizing and co-operating among themselves, that they can get better prices for the goods they have to sell than they could without the organization; and they now come to this parliament to get authority to go a little further in co-operation, in order to cut out the middleman on some of the articles that they use in connection with the operation of their farms. It has been pointed out that they may not succeed if they go into too many lines of business, and that the shareholders may lose in the end. While that is true, why should we sit in judgment and say that 30,000 farmers shall not be allowed to do that if they want to do it? In the final result they have to depend on the honour and honesty and ability of their own men whom they put in charge to carry on this work, just as any other corporation has to do. You cannot take the responsibility away from tbe shareholders. They elect their directors, Mr. CLARKE (Essex).
and they have to abide by the consequences. I have no reason to douibt that this Grain Growers' Grain Association Company will be able to handle the purchasing of the various articles needed by the farmers, and do it as well as they have handled the selling of wheat in the past. They come here and ask for certain powers which are not greater than have been given in dozens of other cases, and I do not think we would be justified in refusing to grant their request. At the same time I think all the restrictions that we impose on other companies should be imposed on this company.
On section 14, subsection (j),
What is section 167 of the Companies' Act?
That provides that the company cannot lend money to its directors.
Why should this company be allowed to do that when other companies cannot?

Their idea, as stated in the committee, was that they might make advances on grain before the crop was ready for the market. The committee has amended the clause so as to limit the amount that they can lend.
There must be a principle involved in 167, I would like to know what it is?
The clause is ' No company shall loan any of its funds to any shareholder.' That is the whole section.
That is very necessary to prevent a great evil-to prevent what we know means fraud. This company has no more right to do that than any other.
The people they are dealing with are almost all members of this company.
That would apply to any company. If a company manufactures or does a banking business or anything else, its own shareholders are its best customers.
Banks can lend money to their own shareholders.

There is a reason for that which does not exist in this case. This company has the power to do everything under the sun, which is all the more reason why there should be some restriction put on it. It may guarantee the performance of contracts by other persons, although we have guarantee companies specially chartered for that purpose.

I think that the clause allowing the company to guarantee the per-

formance of contracts should be struck out.
I would suggest that this clause be allowed to stand over also for consideration. I do not see much objection to authorizing the company to lend money to its shareholders. It might be most desirable for the farmers that they should be able to obtain loans from this company on their warehouse receipts for grain.
Why not restrict the advances to the shipping of grain alone?

That can be considered when we deal with the clause again.
On subsection (1),
Sell or dispose of the undertaking of the company, or any part thereof, for such consideration as the company may think fit, and in particular for shares, debentures or securities of any other company having objects altogether or in part similar to those of the company.
Why emphasize that section by these words 'in particular?'

That is a standard clause in the Act.
On subsection (n),
Do all such other things as are incidental or conducive to the attainments of the objects or purposes of the company.
Can any one tell us what are the objects and purposes of this company?
That is -a standard clause.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 14 is carried with exception of subsections (b), (e) and (f).
On section 15, subsection 2,
Nothing in this section contained shall limit or restrict the borrowing of money by the company on hills of exchange or promissory notes made, drawn, accepted or endorsed by or on behalf of the company.

I am sorry I shall have to oppose this subsection. It makes the borrowing power unlimited. Under the Companies' Act there is a limitation, and the borrowing and issuing of debentures is limited to a certain proportion of the paid up capital stock. I think that under the Companies' Act there is a limitation of the power to issue debentures to a certain portion of the capital stock. If there is not there ought to be. I know there is in the Provincial Joint Stock Companies' Acts. Under the provision now before us, the company might issue debentures for many times the capital stock. The limitation ought not to exceed two-thirds the paid-up capital stock of the company.
I think the lenders will control that.
I would like to have that clause stand to have it amended.
This clause is exactly in the words of the Joint Stock Companies' Act.
I have in mind the New Brunswick Act, which is taken from the Ontario Act. It may have been amended
Yes, formerly it was limited.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 15 stands for further consideration.
On section 17:	Superannuation, pension
funds, &c.,

This section is peculiarly worded.
The company may, on resolution adopted by a vote of shareholders present or represented by proxy at any general meeting ol the company

-and so on. On these conditions they may establish these pension funds. It should provide at least for a two-thirds majority. As it stands it means nothing but a majority of those present.

I would ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), is it usual to give companies powers of this kind? I confess I do not know. It looks to me like affording an opportunity for seme people to vote money into their own pockets under the name of superannuation or pension fund.
It is certainly unusual. I understand the railway companies do it, and the banks.

Why should an omnibus company like this have such powers? That is one of the difficulties in granting these wide and varied powers, it makes every concession granted to the company all the more dangerous.
This seems to be an innovation.
Something new every day.
They justified the general clauses of this Bill by appealing to the Companies' Act. And now, they ask something that is not in the Companies' Act at all.
I think it had better stand.
See what it allows them to do. They need not have the vote of any | particular number of shareholders.
They must be notified.

Yes, but anybody who has had experience in companies knows how easy it is for interested parties to get proxies and carry a vote. I do not think this power should be given at any rate until this company shall have some experience. When it gets into working order, if it wants to come back and get a superannuation system under proper conditions it should have an opportunity to do so.
I would like to see the clause stand until it can be redrafted,- make it conditional upon a vote of two-thirds of the shareholders or something like that:

I do not want, by silence, to seem to agree to that proposition. I do not think that such a power should be given to this company at all. It practically makes it an insurance association. Why should they not have safeguards that are required by other concerns of that kind? Why should there not be, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says, a certain experience of this company sufficiently long for us to know that there is need of this system? I want to find out what this company is really doing before adding this clause.
When you come down to the fact of the matter, what are you doing? By this clause you are making an insurance company without any of the safeguards.
Stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall I report progress, on this Bill? I think, perhaps, I should mention to the committee that any proposed amendments to this Bill should be given notice of lest they should infringe the rule.
Progress reported.

House in committee on Bill (No. 169) to incorporate the Canada West Loan Corporation.
On section 7,

I would like to call the attention of the hon. gentleman who has this Bill in charge, that this section brings up the same thing we have discussed in reference to the Bank Act. As this is a loan company, and is no less important than a bank in many respects, it would seem as if this required more notice:
And no certificate shall be given until the board of directors has been elected as required by this Act, nor until it has been shown to the satisfaction of the Minister of Mr. FOSTER
Finance that at least $500,000 of the capital stock of the company have been subscribed.
The amounts outlined by the Finance Minister for the Bank Act have put in the word ' bona fide ' before the word 'subscribed.' I think these words should be added after the 'capital stock of the company' :
Have been bona fide subscribed, and at least $100,000 thereof have been paid.
That is, of the sum bona fide subscribed. What you want to make sure of is that there should not be a fake subscription, and that the amendment which goes in as a certificate of deposit, should be of actual moneys bona fide subscribed and paid in, and not borrowed on notes and securities, as in the case of the Farmers' Bank.
I do not see any need of it, but I have no objection to the hon. gentleman's suggested amendment. The clause is the usual one which has been inserted in the other company Bills.

Perhaps it does not make any difference provided everything is honestly carried out. But it was thought to be of so much importance that the Finance Minister has outlined that as one of the necessary amendments to the Bank Act; and one can see where it might be made use of if there was a suspicion that things were not properly carried out.

Amendment agreed to.
On section 30,
Why is this company exempted from the requirement to use the word ' limited ' after the name of the company?
It is not usual with loan companies.

I am inclined to think that the word ' limited ' ought to be used to convey to the public thp knowledge that there is not an unlimited liability of the shareholders. Of course, the use of the word ' corporation ' signifies to the public that the company is incorporated, but does not signify that it is limited as to its liability.
The word ' limited ' is not used in connection with financial corporations, such as trust companies and loan companies.

ilar to that of another company, would be apt to tie confused with it, and in the interest of the older company, which has been established in a similar business for several years, and in the interest of the public who are interested in avoiding the confusion of names, my purpose in making the motion was that the Minister of Finance might be aware of this similarity of names.

donell, Toronto) says that the company opposing our name is generally known as ' The Canadian Casualty Company.' That is not our fault. In any case, the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company, I understand, has been bought and is run as a side-show by a Scottish company, known as the General Accident Insurance Corporation. These being the facts, and it being merely a matter of opinion whether the names are similar or not, I think the Bill should be proceeded with.

It has been usual, where there has been a dispute about a name, to get the opinion of the Minister of Finance. I do not see that there would be anything to find fault with if we were to take up all the sections of this Bill except the first, which deals with the name, but to leave that until the Bill could be taken up again with the Minister of Finance here. There is no disposition to prevent the passing of the Bill.

I have made inquiry of the Superintendent of Insurance, who is in attendance, and he tells me that the matter was thoroughly threshed out before the Banking and Commerce Committee, and that it was decided to leave the name exactly as it is. He tells me also that the Minister of Finance has left no information with him that he desires to express any opinion with regard to the recommendation of the committee. I do not see why we might not dispose of the Bill this evening. It seems to me. there is no similarity in the names of these companies, and no likelihood of confusion. What weighs with me is that the committee, after discussion and careful consideration, decided to recommend the Bill with this name.

I was present when this matter was discussed in the Banking and Commerce Committee. The Minister of Finance was not in his place. True, the Finance Department was represented. As my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has pointed out, it is usual, when a similarity of names arises, that the Minister of Finance is questioned in the House with regard to the matter. Surely the hon. member who has charge of the Bills will not press it. If it is not put through tonight that will not interfere with its passage, and it is only fair to the committee to have a statement from the Minister of Finance on the question. Surely, if the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) had looked closely at these names he would not have said that there is no similarity. One company is known as ' The Canadian

Casualty Company,' and the other 'The Casualty Company of Canada.' Surely it will not be said that there is not great similarity between these names. It is usual, as I have said, in cases of this kind, to have a statement from the Minister of Finance.

I certainly think the suggestion of the hon. member from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) should be accepted. The Minister of Finance usually has strong feeling on the question of names of companies. He has on many occasions, both in committee and in the House, expressed himself very clearly and strongly on such matters. And we are all of the opinion that it is unfortunate if the name given to a new company leads to confusion with some existing company. Now with great deference to the Minister of Public Works, I hardly think he is right. The words that catch the ear and arrest the attention are that this company, which we propose to incorporate, is a casualty company and a Canadian company, The Casualty Company of Canada; the other words in reference to boiler insurance are likely in ordinary language to Ibe left out. The company may preserve its identity, it may print all its gapers properly, and sign its letters with the full name of the company; and yet the public, speaking of the company, may abbreviate it and speak of this as The Canadian Casualty Company, although it is a Casualty Company , of Canada, so that after a little while one company will be confused with the other, to the great disadvantage of the companies themselves and of the public. The Minister of Finance has communicated to this company his objection to this incorporation, and we assume that he still maintains his objection. I do not think we should have this unseemly difference in the cabinet; I think the expressed opinion of the Minister of Finance ought to be concurred in.

Do I understand my *hon. friend to say that the Minister of Finance has sent word to this committee of his objections to the Bill? I have not so understood it. If that werq the case, I would yield my view at once to the view of the Minister of Finance.

No; I was saying that the Minister of Finance had expressed himself clearly through his representative in the committee, and we are bound to assume that he is still of the same opinion. That being the case, I think his colleagues in the cabinet ought to defer to his judgment in this matter, as it pertains more especially to his department. I understand that his representative was in the committee and expressed himself as opposed to the name.

That is not correct. In the Senate committee when this Bill was considered, the present name was given to this company, with the consent of the Superintendent of Insurance, the representative of the Finance Department. If I thought that the Minister of Finance was at all opposed to this name, I would not attempt to press the Bill. I do not wish to be discourteous to the hon. member for North Toronto; but the only reason I have for asking that the committee proceed with this Bill is that I have to leave for the west in two or three days, and may not have another opportunity of bringing it forward.

speechtext: I have authority from the Department of Finance to say that the Senate committee examined this very question which is now_under discussion as to whether the name of this company was liable to be confounded with the name of another company, which I understand is the Boiler and Casualty Company; and that the contention that there was a conflict between the names was rejected, and the present name was accepted. I understand also that objection was taken in the committee of this House, and that the present name was accepted upon a division in the committee. I understand that the Superintendent of Insurance was present in the committee as representing the Department of Finance, and that he raised no objection to the present Bill. Therefore it is not exactly correct to say that the Minister of Finance does not concur in this legislation.

Of course I accept the Prime Minister's version of the case as he understands it, but I do not understand him to say that he has had any direct communication with the Minister of Finance in the matter. I am informed by some' gentlemen around me that they understand that the Minister of Finance does not approve of the name.
On what does my hon. friend base that statement?
I am so informed.
I think my hon. friend is misinformed.

I gather it from members of the House in whom I have great confidence. I may say to my hon. friend who is promoting the Bill, that we do not wish tc prevent his Bill going through; I want him to get his Bill through. But I do not think that what is suggested by the member for North Toronto will have the effect of preventing this Bill going through. We will probably reach it again before he leaves.
