I do not think any members of the House whom the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has spoken of as informing him that the Minister of Finance is opposed to the Bill, will get up in their places and say that they have heard him so express himself. The member for Simcoe argued a few minutes ago that there ought not to be any division in the cabinet on this matter, and that because the representative of the Minister of Finance is opposed to the name, therefore the other members of the cabinet ought also to be opposed to it.
It is not as bad as that.

Now when he finds that the superintendent of insurance, representing the Minister of Finance, expressed himself favourably to the name, will he still think that there ought not to be a division in the cabinet, although the committee did agree with the opinion thus obtained?

I think there is a valid objection to the name, no matter what the opinion of the Minister of Finance is, and also no matter what confusion may arise with the name of any other company. The name which is proposed for this company is simply the Casualty Company of Canada. Now the casualty business is one line of business, the banking business is another line, the trust business is another line, and so on all through the commercial life of the country. It seems to me it would be well to forbid any company using a name like this in any line of business. The Minister of Finance set a good example in connection with a bank which proposed to (monopolize the name The Bank of Canada. It would also be just as objectionable to incorporate a company calling itself The Trust Company of Canada, whether there was any other similar named' company in existence or not. It would seem to me also to afford an unfair advantage to any other company to be allowed to call itself The Loan Company of Canada, or to any set of incorporators to be called The Life Insurance Company of Canada. In all these cases I think so comprehensive a name gives them an undue advantage over other similar companies. So, even though there were no other companies, or no special circumstances, the better course for (this parliament to pursue would be to forbid to any company so unfair an advantage as would be given by allowing them to use this name. But in this case there is an additional objection. There is a company now in existence known as the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company. That is an additional objection, but in the very nature of things a similar objection would lie to almost any attempt to assume so comprehensive a name as this. For instance if a company asked to be known as the Life Mr. LENNOX.
Insurance Company of Canada, objection would at once be taken that there would be confusion with the Canada Life Assurance Company. It is argued by the hon. member for Eegina (Mr. Martin) that because the first company, the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company, has the additional ' Boiler Insurance Company5, it is distinguishable. No doubt to a lawyer and those familiar with the company it is very readily distinguishable, but as the hon. member knows, the general public do not like writing long names, and as a matter of fact, the company will be known by the first part of its name almost invariably. I have been furnished with a series of envelopes selected out of one mail of the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company. Seven of these are addressed to the Canadian Casualty Company, Toronto, and one of them is a letter ad-, dressed in typewriting from another large" company in Toronto, so it can easily be understood how the ordinary man would address them. The hon. member for Eegina (Mr. Martin) says that is not the fault of the applicants for this Bill. Certainly it is not, who would suggest it was? But it is similarly not the fault of this company. I am instructed that this company never signs itself or refers to itself as the 'Canadian Casualty Company, but ilJ ,is rooted in human nature that they should be so addressed. There will inevitably be confugion, and that confusion means a direct financial loss to the existing company. The Minister of Finance strongly opposed the use of a_ comprehensive title like this in the case of a bank, and he was upheld by the House. Surely there could be no objection to the name applied for by the incorporators of the bank now known as the Banque Nationale of Canada that will not apply to this one. If the Minister of Finance had a policy at that time, the same policy must apply in this case. We should not allow any company in any line of business to say that it was the company of that line of business of Canada, We should adopt that as a first principle in legislation of this kind. If there was some other adjective such as the Casualty and Guarantee Company of Canada the objection would be partly overcome, but a casualty business is one line of business, and no company should be allowed to say that it is the Casualty Company of Canada. To my mind that is the extreme limit of error.

I differ from the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). I think the distinction is sufficiently clear, and if the present casualty company allowed themselves to be called by the two first words of their name, and they write letters or allow themselves to be so addressed without calling atten-

tion to the error, it is their fault. I think the House is going too far in the direction in which my hon. friend would lead it, it is too exacting already. Casualty is a general term, and in how many companies do we find such general terms, as British, Canadian, Western, Eastern, Northern, Dominion, National? I suppose casualty means no more than insurance, a casualty contract would be an indemnity contract, and when we see those two names written on sign boards, one the Casualty Company of Canada, and the other the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company, there is no confusion. I would favour giving this name. I think the applicants are entitled to it, and that those objecting have not shown a sufficient cause.

It would be well, perhaps, to ascertain how these people lit upon this name. In the first place, in their published advertisement of their intention to apply for this Bill they gave the name of Lloyd's Casualty Company. In that they were treading on the corns of Lloyd's Limited and Lloyd's Limited appeared before the Senate Committee and objected. This Bill was initiated in the Senate. In the Senate Committee the objection was taken, and it was quite apparent it was well taken, and the promoters of this Bill cast about to find some other name. In a moment, before the committee and without any published notice to anybody, without notice to the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company or anybody else, this name was settled upon and taken.
It is absurd-that is a strong word to use, but I think it is well applied-it is absurd to say that there is no similarity between these two names. This company seeks incorooration under the name of the Casualty Company of Canada, and the name of the old company is the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company, and as has been abundantly proven the Canadian Casualty and Boiler Insurance Company is known generally to the public as the Canadian Casualty Company and is very generally addressed that way through the mail. The hardship of passing the Bill in this shape is that you have this old insurance company engaged in the casualty business in the city of Toronto, and this new company, proposing to embark in an identically similar business, with its head office in the same city, takes a name that is bound to be confused with the other. There is no reason whatever why these people should want to be incorporated under this name unless it be that they desire to acquire the name for the purpose of sharing in the good will of the business of the existing company. I am not suggesting that, but it certainly looks as though such were
the case. This House may not have much to do with the confusion that may arise in the business of the two companies, but it certainly has to do with the protection of the public and in the public interest such a name should not be given the new company. There is, of course, the larger objection that this House would never incorporate a company under the name of the ' The Bailway Company of Canada ' or ' The Steamship Company of Canada,' and there is no reason why they should incorporate an insurance company under such a name. The Minister of Finance has years of experience in dealing with just such cases as this, and I am satisfied that if he were here he would share my opinion. I do not agree with the statement of the chairman of the committee that the Finance Department agreed to this name. The Bill was before the committee twice; on the first occasion the representative of the department was adverse, and on the last occasion when he was asked squarely what was his opinion he said he had no opinion to offer. There is no desire to force these people into any particular name, but I think they should make their reputation under their own name and not under the name of a company established in business.
If the chairman of the . Banking and Commerce Committee will say that the Minister of Finance has been consulted and that he offered no objection to this name I will be 'satisfied.

On section 8,
8. The property and assets of Revillon Brothers, Limited, to be vested in the company incorporated by this Act shall be deemed to be and consist of the properties specified in the schedule to this Act; but nothing in this Act shall affect the rights of any creditors of the said Revillon Brothers, Limited.

I would like to call the attention of the committee to this section, also to sections 6, 9 and 11. In the first place, I presume the committee has considered the matter, and I would hesitate to criticise their action in passing this Bill. But it strikes me as about as extraordinary a Bill as 1 have ever seen. This Bill purports to vest by Act of parliament all the assets of another company in a new company, and it repeals the charter of the old company, it revokes and annuls the letters patent, and repeals the statute passed in 1906 confirming these letters patent.
Is that the new company or the same?

Another company. Each company has a separate existence and may have separate liabilities. Then by section 9 it seems to recognize another company; still it is a company incorporated in France, and whose assets are alleged by this Bill to be handed over to the new company, whereas this Bill 271
does not hand over the assets of the French company at all, but only the assets of the company which was incorporated by letters ipatent in 1904. In this case it may be all right, there may be no creditors, but what we do to-day may be a precedent for legislation to-morrow. Suppose there was a man who had a claim against the existing company and a suit was pending; the moment this statute comes into force the charter of the existing company is annulled, its letters patent become void, the statute recognizing these letters is repealed, and there is no old company in existence; so the man would find himself out of court at once. It is true his rights are protected by a provision that this company shall be liable for th6 debts of the old company, but every man's suit would be discontinued. It seems to me the proper course would be to authorize the existing company, to convey their properties to the new company by the proper conveyance, and then make this company liable for the debts of the existing company, and make provision that any suits pending might be carried to a conclusion in the name of the old company, but that the new company should be liable for judgments which might be obtained. But by this statute we wipe out at once, by a stroke of the pen when this statute comes into force, the charter of the old company, and wipe out all suits that might be pending. It strikes me as entirely new legislation, and objectionable.

I was on the committee when this Bill was brought up, and I certainly felt as the Minister of Public-Works has just said. The applicants for the Bill were two gentlemen of very high professional reputation, Mr. Lafleur and Mr. Mc-Dougall, and there was an indisposition to doubt the correctness of the measure, because these gentlemen were vouching for it. The whole story was of the most intricate character. There had been two blunders, apparently, in the course of the existence of these companies. The first charter appeared to be a blunder, then there was another blunder, and this was an effort to redeem the two blunders, and put .the corporations upon another footing. Feeling the importance of the matter, I suggested in the committee that we should appoint a committee of four legal gentlemen to act with the counsel and go over this Bill with extreme care, and see that now, after all the troubles they had been involved in, we did not make another and a worse blunder still. I do not think it was possible for any member of the committee clearly to understand what they were doing. I have no doubt whatever that the promoters of the Bill, the legal gentlemen present, were strictly truthful in everything they said, and said nothing they did not know. But I think also that the committee were re-



*sponsible, and I felt that we ought not to act entirely on the opinion of the legal gentlemen present. I was not able, on the statements made there, either to approve or disapprove of the Bill. I can only say that as a member of that committee, and now sitting in the House, I have no more idea whether the passing of the Bill will produce the result that was intended, than I have as to whether there are inhabitants in Mars. I doubt whether any member of the committee thoroughly understood it. It was passed largely upon the reputation of the two legal gentlemen who were present, and who had been acting all through for the Revillon Freres Trading Company, Limited. There is a Revillon Freres in France, and there is a chartered Revillon Brothers under a charter issued by the Secretary of State, and there is now this Bill. Who will be who by and by, I do not know. I am not surprised that the minister is in doubt about it, and I do hot think that any member of the committee has the slightest idea what it means. I think that for the sake of the reputation of parliament something should be done. I do not think we are justified in passing legislation that we do not understand. I think it ought to be referred to a special committee, who would report to the general committee. That is what I suggested before, but my view was not accepted by the committee.

speechtext: If anything comes from Mars, my hon. friend the Minister of Customs will look after it, I know. The promoter of the Bill not being here, I suggest that the committee rise and report progress.

I can fully endorse everything my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has said. It was the most confused Bill I ever saw come before the committee, and I think the committee were just about as confused after the Bill was [DOT] Mr. BARKER.
passed as when we took it up. I think it would be advisable for this committee to take some step to put this Bill in a form that it would be workable, at any rate.
I do not think there was a member present in the committee who wanted to interfere with the Bill; we only wanted to do what was right, but wq did not know what we were doing.

As I understand it, the Revillon Freres were a French company having a charter and doing business in many countries in Europe. They desired to do business in Canada, and they applied to the Secretary of State under the Companies1 Act for a charter. That charter was granted, and it was a very peculiar charter, a copy of which was produced before the committee. The charter stated that all the property of Revillon Freres, the French firm, should thereafter be vested in Revillon Brothers, the Canadian company. It did not even limit the property so vested to the Canadian property, but that all the property of Revillon Freres should be vested in Revillon Brothers, the Canadian company. I asked Mr. Lafleur the solicitor for the promoters why they did not ask for legislative authority to have the Canadian company convey their Canadian property to the new *company. It appears that when Revillon Brothers were incorporated in 1904 there was no application filed, that there were no provisional directors named, and that the charter vested the property of Revillon Freres in the Canadian company, but the Canadian company had no entity and no directors who could convey the property. The French company is really the whole company. They supplied all the caprtal, they did business in Canada under the name of Revillon Brothers, under a charter granted by the Secretary of State and without any one finding fault for a number of years. The Bank of Montreal who were their bankers suddenly said:	We do not think you
have the right to carry on business in this way, and we will not advance you any further money because the charter granted by the Secretary of State conveys nothing to anybody, there being no directors, and they have never organized and could never organize under that charter. They answered: We will get the French company to endorse our paper, but the bank said:	That
is worthless because the French company have vested all their property in the Canadian company, and, therefore, it is divested from them and nobody has it. It was absolutely impossible for the Canadian company to reconvey, and the only thing that could be done was to get this Act of parliament vesting the property in the ' new company.
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) had better sleep over it, and find another explanation.
My hon. friend might not understand it, but most members of the committee did.

I do understand that, according to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) the Dominion government issued a charter to nobody for nothing. They granted a charter to a company which had no directors provisional or otherwise.
That is quite right.

And consequently it was not worth the paper it was written on, and yet it was given to conduct a large business. That is pretty good proof that there is something wrong in a department which would issue such a charter.

I am not defending the charter; I am simply stating the facts.
Progress reported.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I wish to call the attention of the Minister of the Interior in his capacity as Superintendent General of Indian Affairs to a matter that has been brought to my notice quite recently. It has reference to certain damage done by a fire caused by a steam threshing machine operated by government officials
85S7

on Pasqua's Indian Reserve, which is situate! near Fort Qu'Appelle, on the 29th of October, 1910. At the time the threshing was taking place the wind was blowing a perfect gale. Practically all the machines in the neighbourhood shut down though another fire was caused by one of the machines which continued threshing that day. The fire, according to my informant, burned the separator, and was allowed to run out over the country, doing damage which was estimated by the North West Mounted Police to amount to between $8,000 and $10,000. Mr. Nichol, the Indian Agent, who at the time was in charge of the machine, was summoned by the North West Mounted Police for allowing the fire to run at large. He appeared before a justice of the peace at Fort Qu'Appelle, and was fined the sum of $25 for the offence. My informant informs me that the inspector of Indian Agencies, Mr. W. M. Graham, took occasion to go through the district and inquire as to the amount of damage which had been caused by the fire which took place after the burning of the machine. It is stated that he made an estimate of the losses, and sent that estimate to Ottawa. Several settlers made application to be reimbursed for the losses they sustained; and the only word they had from Ottawa was to the effect that the department did not consider themselves responsible. Now, it is well known all through the North West that it is a very dangerous thing to continue threshing with a steam threshing outfit when there is a very high wind blowing. On such occasions very few farmers will allow threshing to go on, as the number of accidents that occur from that cause are very numerous; but when such accidents do occur, the responsibility is placed on the owner of the threshing machine to see that all damages which result to the people are paid. In the same neighbourhood as the case I mention a fire starting from a threshing machine of Mr. Guy May got away and burned several bins of wheat and oats belonging to his neighbours, and he had to pay for the damages done. Mr. May had some excuse, perhaps, for threshing on that particular day. It seems that he had only five acres of crop to finish his whole season's work, and on such occasions men will try to finish their threshing. But I am rather at a loss to understand why a government official should consider it necessary to take risks under such circumstances, and to continue threshing on a day on which the wind was so extremely high. The fire in question burned out a number of settlers in the neighbourhood.
I have a list of some of them, but not a complete list. Three of those settlers have written to me asking me to try to get the government to consider the losses they ' Mr. LAKE.
have sustained and to reimburse them. It seems to me that when a fire of that sort is caused by the recklessness or carelessness of a government official, the government who employ that official should be in the same position as the owner of a private threshing machine, who in .similar cases.is required to reimburse those who suffer loss in consequence of his recklessness or neglect. One of my correspondents writes me to this effect: "
I have practically lost all my grain and buildings, and it seems strange that I cannot get common justice from the Interior Department, when it was proved that it was their employees who caused it. This is the second time that I have lost grain and buildings by fire from the same cause. I came to Canada from England with a little capital and bought this farm. Now I have nearly lost it all by these fires.
Another man wrote to me that he had lost two-thirds of his crop, which was threshed and in the granaries. Yet another writes about the considerable losses that he sustained. I know that settlers living in the neighbourhood of Indian reserves frequently suffer very seriously from fires which accidently or carelessly start on these reserves. I presume this is due mainly to the fact that there are very few settlers on the reserve, and a very small amount of land is broken up, and the fires get great headway before they are brought under control. In this particular case the fire started from a threshing machine which was being operated by an employee of the government, who was threshing the grain of the Indians. The fire must have been a terrible one because it jumped across both railway tracks at a point where there is a siding and continued unchecked on the other side of the line. I thought, it necessary to bring this matter up to-day as rumors are current that the government are likely to move an adjournment or prorogation before very long; and it is only within the last day or two that the facts have come into my possession and the sufferers have asked me to bring this matter up. This fire occurred in the end of last October, and it is very desirable that the payment of damages should not be delayed. If these people have suffered these losses owing to the fault of the government, they should be reimbursed immediately. A great deal of hardship has been inflicted on a number of innocent individuals, and they consequently are perfectly entitled to compensation just as much as they would be, had the fire been set by the owner of a private threshing machine or some one in his employ. I hope the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs (Mr. Oliver) will have the matter looked into and give orders that the government pay whatever damages have been inflicted.

Like my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) I have a good deal of sympathy with the farmers who suffered such severe loss by the prairie fire that started on the Indian reserve. This matter was brought to my attention some two or three months ago, and-I at once wrote the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. I wrote to him on two or three occasions giving him all the facts. In my opinion, under similar circumstances a private individual who owned that threshing machine would be responsible, because there was evidently negligence on the part of those who were handling it. But unfortunately the government does not stand in the same position as a private individual in respect of damages. On referring to the file in connection-with this matter, I find that it was referred by the Indian Department to the Justice Department, and the following opinion was given by the latter:
Sir,-Eeplying to your letter of the 15th 'December, 1910, in which you request to be advised whether your department is liable for the claims of various persons for loss of property by fire which originated, it is alleged, from the negligence of those in charge of a threshing outfit on the Qu'Appelle Agency, Saskatchewan, I have the honour to say that I am not aware of any grounds on which your department could be held liable for such negligence, if proven.
There is, therefore, a great difference between the liabilities of a private individual in a case-of this-kind and the liability of the government. Not having met with much success in the Indian Department, I saw the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) who took the position that the department did not want to shelter itself behind a technicality of the law, but would be willing to pay damages if they were assessed. The great difficulty, however, even if negligence were proven, lay in the assessing of the damages. Were an action in damages brought against the government in the Exchequer Court it would not succeed; but it is possible that an action against the man who was running the threshing machine-and running it on a day when the wind was so high that it was absolute folly to do so-would hold good; and the Minister of the Interior was good enough on one occasion to suggest that if an action were brought against this man, and he was held responsible, the department would stand behind him, and pay the damages. Of course when a man has had his crop destroyed by fire, the crop is always worth twice as much as he would have realized out of it. The whole difficulty is in the assessment of the damages, and that is the position taken by the department to-day.
I cannot see on what grounds the Deputy Minister of Justice distinguishes between the liability of an individual who is running the machne and the liability of the owner of the machine.
The difference is this, that the government cannot be held responsible for wrong done by one of its servants, unless there be some statutory obligation.
That seems to be the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, but upon what authority does he base it? I do not know of any such distinction.
What is the distinction?
That when the government employs an agent to operate a machine, and that machine causes damages, the agent would be responsible but not the government.

On the well known principle that the King can do no wrong.
Mr- LAKE. What practical steps would the Minister of the Interior suggest that these settlers should take? The fire caused a great amount of damages and suffering to these individuals, and that fire was due to the fault of a government employee. I would ask the minister what action these sufferers should take, in order to prove their loss and be paid compensation p_______

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) Has said, 1 nave had several discussions with him, and the conclusion arrived at was that in order to avoid the difficulty which was stated by the Department of Justice to stand in the way. the parties should take proceedings directly against the individual at fault, who was in charge of the machine, and was also an employee of the government, with the understanding that any damages assessed against him the government will be prepared to pay on getting a vote from parliament. The position is an unfortunate one in which the settler stands at present, but it is one we ourselves cannot avoid, the law being as it is. JBut by the procedure that 1 suggest, it seems to me that would be avoided, and the payment of the claim would be a matter of policy which 1 would recommend the government to recommend to the House and, for which I am sure, the House would provide in due course. I wish it distinctly understood that the department does not wish, as a matter of policy, to avoid the responsibility which would rest upon it if, instead of a department it was an individual and damage had resulted to private citizens from any act for which it is responsible.

The difficulty about settling and awarding damages as a departmental matter must strike any one who gives the subject attention. It is not wise for any branch of the government to undertake to adjudicate over its own matters which, under other circumstances, would be decided on by an action in court. There is room for all sorts of discussion as to motives, and as to the result which would be achieved by such procedure; and it seems to me that, in the interest of both the country on the one hand and of the sufferers on the other hand, the responsibility should be decided by an impartial tribunal, and amount of damages should be assessed by such a tribunal. Such a tribunal, of course, are the courts of the country, if the matter can be brought before them; and it seems to me the matter can be brought before them in the way i suggest. At first, as the House has been informed, the question was asked the Department. of Justice: Can we deal with this matter in the ordinary course? We were informed we could not. The matter was then taken up for further consideration with the result I have indicated

The principle that the Crown is not responsible for the negligence of its servants has been very largely cut down by legislation in this country, in connection with the operation of the Intercolonial railway and m connection with public works. And I do not think it has been further extended by statute, certainly not so far as I am aware. As to the case to which the minister refers, it is highly probable that the servant guilty of the negligence himself would be liable. But what the minister suggests, I understand, is that action should be brought against him. and then the Crown should take into consideration whether they should pay?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

That does not seem a very satisfactory or definite attitude. In the first place, if these men have suffered damages by the negligence of another person, that damage ought to be made good, even though the person who caused it was a servant of the Crown when he did it. There is no reason why this fajrmer should be out of pocket by reason of the negligence of another person, simp'iy because that other person happened to be a servant of the Crown. Some person ought to reimburse him; and, if the Crown is disposed to take cognizance of the matter, they ought to say: Co on and make your case against this man who was acting as our servant, and if you make out that he was guilty of negligence in the course of Mr. OLIVER.
his work, we will see that it is paid, and the cost of the action also. It does not seem to me to be dealing with this farmer in a fair way to say, after he has gone to the trouble and expense of an action against the party: We will take it into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish to be understood as leaving the matter in the position which my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has suggested. But he understands that in my place 1 cannot bind the government, nor can I bind parliament to vote the money. But I am, on the responsibility of my position, stating what is the policy of the government in this particular case. And, of course, that is binding upon the government so .far as its recommendation to parliament is concerned. If we could go further I would be glad to do it, but that is as far as I can go, and I should think it -would be satisfactory.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax) If the minister means that the government will submit an estimate to parliament of the amount of damage, that is perfectly satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

If I understand he is simply dealing with the technical consideration that he is not able to bind parliament, yet I think the government undertakes to bind parliament with matters of more importance, or rather, not undertakes to bind parliament, but undertakes to submit to parliament and carry through, which is much the same thing.

Might I suggest, as a way out of this difficulty, that if the department is satisfied that this is a case deserving of compensation, and in view of the fact that a collective action could not be brought, but that there would have to be separate or individual action on behalf of every one of these farmers, which would mean great expense, the government, instead of going through the forms of trial in each case, should appoint an assessor to assess the damages for all the farmers and then submit an estimate to parliament to pay these damages. That would avoid the trouble of individual trial. And some of these people may not be in a position to incur the expense of a trial. But if the government, recognizing its liability, would take the course I suggested I think it would overcome the difficulty.
_ Mr. OLIVER. While the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Porter) could be adopted, I do not think it is wise, as I have already said, either in the interests of the country or in the interests of the claimant, that the amount of the damages should be settled in that way. I am satisfied that my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) who sits beside

the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) will suggest to him that if the government undertook to make an assessment of the damages, the assessment might be varied according to the political predilections of the claimant rather than the merits of the case. I think it is fairer to everybody and in everybody's interest that there should be full opportunity given to have the matter brought to court and tried out in the ordinary way, so that there may be no question about the rights of the country or of the individual being affected by anything b.ut the merits of the case.
Is the negligence admitted?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; I forgot to mention that point. There is no actual admission of negligence in the proceedings that have gone forward so far against the man who operated the engine. When the fire took place a summons was issued against the agent of the reserve; he was brought up and pleaded guilty and was fined $25. But the agent was not on the reserve on that day, so that his plea of guilty, while it may have had some merit in some way, did not really bear upon the point, it did not bring the question to an issue. It was a general allegation, and he made a general plea of guilty. But my hon. friend will understand that it was not a satisfactory solution of the question. The question of whether~the man who ran the engine was directly responsible, has not really been tried-nut yet.- -
Would not the fact that a high gale was blowing at the time be sufficient evidence of negligence? Any one knowing that country would say so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That question illustrates my point. .Courts exist for the purpose of doing justice between man and man, that is their primary object, and that question was the very question the courts should decide; it should not be- a question of the judgment of one of the interested parties.

It seems to me the minister puts the case in this w*ay: There has been damage done to some farmers, and he will not take the trouble to investigate for himself, and ascertain vdiether tire government is responsible, but the proper way is for the courts to decide the question. That is very well for the legal profession, they must have every case fought out in court, with law costs for the plaintiff and law costs for the defendant, and then the government will pay the damages. Why should not the minister inquire into the facts, and if he finds there is negligence why should he call a jury to pass upon it? That question comes up
every day with railway companies, and they have to pay. They do not insist upon providing law costs on both sides of the case before they pay. Surely the hon. gentleman can take the trouble to ascertain whether the agent of the government was wrong or not, and if he finds he was wrong he will pay these damages.

This is one of the special cases in which the minister might depart from what he says is a general rule, and a very good rule. The minister says that as a general rule it is not a good thing for the government to take matters of this kind in hand, and settle them without a lawsuit to establish the liability, and the amount of damages. The minister says he has not actually admitted the liability, and technically he has not. His agent admitted liability, and was fined, but he was not there when the fine occurred, and negligence consequently has not been established. There is tire fact, I understand, of a very high gale, and it was negligence to run the machine at all in such a gale. Now, if the minister is satisfied that it is a case in which the government ought to pay these people, he does not need to stand on technicalities. This matter has been before the House and the House I think is of the ODinion that there ought to be compensation. Why then have a lawsuit about it? I would suggest that the minister have an investigation to ascertain the facts. Let him appoint a judge to look into this matter. I think there has been sufficient negligence to justiiy^the- country in paying these-farmers. If the minister thinks that there has been negligence, then he need not refer that point to the judge, but let him refer the question of how much damages in each case was sustained. I would not under such circumstances recommend the minister to refer the question of negligence to the judge, but to ask the judge to take evidence as to the amount of damages. It has been suggested to me that a farmer might recover only $200 or $300. But there are some farmers who cannot bring an action at all, and when the minister is here, and has the whole parliament as his advisers. I think he can act upon their advice and make this an exceptional case.

I am at loss to understand how my 'hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) who is a good lawyer, could undertake to say that he has heard enough about this case to give judgment upon it, and that the minister would be justified in dispensing with the usual preliminaries of legal proceedings before he settles these claims. If the Department of Justice has investigated this matter thoroughly, and has advised that there is no negligence, then there is no right of action.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) if the facts are as he understands them, that is that the Department of Justice has advised that there is no negligence. I understood that all the Justice Department were consulted about was the question of liability on the technical point as to whether the government were liable for the negligence of their servant, and that they advised they were not. If the Department of Justice took the facts into consideration, and said on the evidence as well as the law that there was no liability it would assume a different position.

I have here the letter of Mr. Newcombe, in which he says:
I have the honour to say that I am not aware of any grounds on which your department could be held liable for such negligence, if proven.
The opinion of the Department of Justice upon that question seems to me to close the door as far as the minister is concerned, and the proposition he has made appears to me very reasonable. When dealing with this question of claims, it is all very well to say: It is a good general rule, but we must make an exception. I do not think that, sitting here as members of parliament apd hearing the facts presented, ably as they were, by the hon. member for Qu'-Appelle, we are able to form a judgment which ought to be arrived at only by a court of competent jurisdiction which could determine whether there was negligence as a matter of fact or within the law. My hon. friends cannot blow hot and cold. We frequently hear them complain that the departments have settled claims by appointing commissioners, but here is a ease where the minister takes the course they have advocated. The minister is prepared to treat these gentlemen fairly and to recognize any verdict given in the case after a thorough investigation by a court. That is the proper way to deal with claims, and it is not right to make exceptions.
Would the hon. member say from the papers who paid the fine?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The fine has not been paid.

Every one understands that the Crown is not liable for the negligence of its servants; we got beyond that an hour ago. The minister was considering what he could do in case negligence was proven by a servant of the Crown, by submitting an estimate to parliament.
The question was whether there was any negligence.

1 agree for the moat part that the Crown should determine Mr. MACDONALD.
these matters by some tribunal. On the other hand if there was a perfectly plain case, if the negligence was so clear that no question of its existence could be raised, it would foe of no use to send the matter to the courts, if for instance a man took off his spark arrester in a gale.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because it was, a windy day it does not follow that negligence is established. My information is that the thresher was working in the shelter of the woods, and for that reason it was believed to be safe. If that is the case, there is sufficient doubt to warrant it being referred to court.
In case the courts found there was no negligence, then would the minister do anything to help the farmers, or drop the case? As a matter of equity, the farmers should be compensated.
The discussion is very irregular at this stage, and I will have to stop it.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS ON THE NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
LABOUR CONDITIONS ON THE NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Labour to an item in the Toronto ' News ' of Saturday. It is headed:
Robbing Foreign Labourers on the Transcontinental Railway-Startling charges from Port Arthur that stores are used to swindle hard-working foreigners who leave in debt after months of toil.
The article states that labourers are advertised for, $2.50 a day being offered. Upon arrival at the point where they are directed to apply they are told there is no employment. Then whilst they are deliberating, it is suggested to them that not being able to obtain work in the ordinary way at wages, they had better become subcontractors, and that a few of them should band together as subcontractors. They agree and then work for weeks and months, perhaps for six months, under a contractor as subcontractors. During that time, they get their supplies at a small store which belongs to the ccntractor. These facts are said to have been ascertained by the counsel at Port Arthur, who investigated the matter and obtained a considerable amount of evidence. The ' News ' states that it has in its. possession a good deal of material upon which to found its article, that these men, after moving solid rock and loose rock and all the rest of it for six months, working harder and longer than they would by the day, and imagining they are making money, finish their contract, their account is made up, they are credited for the work they have done and debited

lor the supplies they have received, and the result is that they are found not to be entitled to anything but are in debt. It is said that the contractor generally comes to the rescue to the extent, that being anxious to get rid of them he transports them to civilization, adding the cost of their pass. age to their indebtedness. Thus, having worked for six or seven months very hard, they receive practically no compensation. The " News ' says they have copies of these accounts in their possession, and adds:
This is the story which the Port Arthur council will tell to the Labour Department at Ottawa. The story will be substantiated by all the figures, contract forms, &c., of a representative case. The foreigners in the particular case to be submitted to the Labour Department bought ten cakes of rough soap, a very laudable thing to do.
For this soap they were charged ten cents per cake, almost enough to make them cease using that article altogether.
Shovels cost these men at the stores $2.50 each; one sack of potatoes, $4; hour, $6; coarse towels, 80 cents a pair; a tin dipper, $1; jam, $1.05 a pail; dynamite, for two cases, $21; lamp chimneys, 25 cents, and so on through a long list with one overcharge piled upon another.
I hope there will be a thorough investigation into these statements in this newspaper. This is not by any means the first rumour that the workmen are being swindled by the contractors, and if there is found to be any foundation for that rumour, I trust the investigation will be general.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS ON THE NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I had a case in court only two weeks ago, the action being between a contractor and three subcontractors and the facts as stated in this newspaper were sworn to by witnesses and corroborated by the accounts produced in court. The contractors took the work at a certain price, re-let to subcontractors, furnished them with supplies and material, and when at the end of the operation a statement of account was asked for, each of the three sub-contractors was found to be in debt rather than having anything to his credit.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS ON THE NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Cases of this kind have been brought to the attention of the department, and on investigation the complaints have been reported to be well founded in some cases and the contractors obliged to redress the grievances, while in other cases there appeared to have been much exaggeration. I have no notice that the particular complaint referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) has as yet been brought to the attention of the department. I have seen some reference to it in the newspapers, and I had intended having it looked into irrespective of a formal complaint, but as a rule it is advisable that the government should wait until its attention is directed to these difficulties. The government has recognized the necessity of a somewhat closer supervision of these construction camps, and an appropriation has been passed for the appointment of one or two officers whose duty it will be to look into just such cases as this.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS ON THE NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I will be pleased to give the minister the names of the contractor and subcontractor in the case I have mentioned.

Royal North West Mounted Police-pay of force, $340,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is the same vote as last year except that the pay of the force is increased by $10,000 and the subsistence by $10,000.
How many men are there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Six hundred and forty-nine men, but this vote is estimated for 700 men which we intend to have.
Mr. LAKE What is paid by the two provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Seventy-five thousand dollars each.
Some of the force lost their lives recently on a trip to the Yukon. I have not been able to understand why they were sent on this journey. Will the Prime Minister explain?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The policy has been to keep a constant patrol in the remote parts of the Dominion-the Hudson Bay, the mouth of the Mackenzie river, Fort Churchill, Fort McPherson-which patrol carries the mail and gathers information. We have been very lucky up to the present time; this is the first casualty.
Inspector Fitzgerald was a native of Halifax, and had very long and very distinguished service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
The unfortunate fatality is greatly to be regretted. What is the distance between the two posts they were travelling between?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Three hundred and fifty miles from*Fort McPherson to Dawson.-Inspector Fitzgerald was a very good officer, and the men under him were good men.	.
Do I understand that these men were making the trip in the ordinary discharge of their duty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Can the department say what was the cause of the fatality?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The diaries kept by the men have been received at Regina and are now on their way to Ottawa. They will give the particulars.
Subsistence, forage, fuel, light, clothing, contingencies, &c., $341,666.67.

* Is the number of the
force increasing or diminishing?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has remained stationary for the last five or six years. We thought at one time that it would be possible to decrease the force, as the provinces might take over their municipal police business. But we find a great reluctance on the part of the settlers in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta to see the force reduced in any way. It is difficult for us to reduce it. We are under contract with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan by which they pay us $75,000 each per year for the services of the police. I am afraid we may have to increase the force, because, as settlers go in beyond the limits of the provinces the force has to be extended. Settlement is now going on north of Edmonton in the Peace river and Mackenzie River districts, and I am sure that we shall have to extend the force in those two districts. Whether we shall be able to reduce it I have serious doubts. At the present time the men are distributed as follows:	In Alberta, five
divisions and ninety-nine detachments; in Saskatchewan, four divisons and eighty-nine detachments; in the Yukon, one division and ten detachments; in the Northwest Territories, one division and five detachments. A division is a settled place in which there is an officer and several men; a detachment consists of one or two or three policemen at a particular point. These men are in the midst of the settlers, ready to give information on almost every point, and to assist them in various ways. For instance, if a settler loses an animal, he goes to a policeman, and the policeman looks after it. If a fire takes place, the settlers go to the police for assistance. In a multitude of ways the police are of great utility to the settlers. Under present circumstances, if any change takes place, it will be in the direction of increasing rather than diminishing the force.
Mr. PORTEE^ I have heard the force spoken of with great commendation; but in travelling through that country it has occurred to me that as the provinces be-Sir WILFRID LAUHIER
come more settled, the officers might be more and more transferred to the outlying districts, and in that way the force might be decreased.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I also have travelled in the two provinces, and I have not yet heard it suggested that the force should be diminished at all in either of the provinces. On the contrary, I think it was suggested that if we were to reduce the force which we have in these two provinces, there would be loud protests.
What oath of office, if any, is required from the officers of the force? What I wish to know particularly is, are any aliens employed on the force?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, British subjects only.
What is the nature of the oath that a man has to take on enrollment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The oath of allegiance, nothing else.
I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman what is the number of the patrol at the head of Lake Winnipeg, and what are their duties?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have a force stationed at Hudson bay, and in winter time the patrol is from Hudson bay t-o Lake Winnipeg.
What is the distribution of the force?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the Hudson Bay district, 12 men, no .horses, 41 dogs-they are at Churchill and Fullerton; in Athabasca and Mackenzie district, 39 men, 34 horses, 27 dogs; in the Regina district, 192 men, -in the Maple Creek district, 39 men; in the Dauphin district, 60 men; in the Battleford district, 38 men; in the Macleod district, 63 men; in the Calgary district, 40 men; in the Prince Albert district, 66 men; in the Edmonton district, 51 men; in the Lethbridge district, 12 men. So that the whole force is practically distributed all over the continent, from Macleod near the boundary line up to the mouth of the Mackenzie river, to Hudson bay and Dawson city.
What particular use is made of the men at Regina, Calgary, Macleod and other cities and large towns?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The station at Regina is the central station for all the force. At a station like Maple Creek there is an inspector, and a body of men, and there are a certain number of stations throughout the district with one or two or three meh at each station, all under the command of and in touch with one officer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The whole distribution of the force is absolutely in the hands of Commander Perry, the commissioner.
of men at each station according as there may be crime, or fear of raid or invasion by cattle raiders, and the force is increased or decreased at each place according to the judgment of the commissioner. Sometimes we are asked to send a contingent where there is trouble expected on account of a strike. There is no fixed rule as to how the force is to be moved. That is 'left to the judgment of the officer in charge.

What I do not quite understand is this: Take Regina, a city of 20,000. amd Calgary, a city of 40,000, why should you have detachments oi the police there? If there be any place in the Northwest where the people should be able to take care of themselves as in eastern Canada it should be in those large centres. I thoroughly appreciate the very great importance of this force, and the great work it has done, and I am not suggesting that it should be decreased, -but I do not understand why we should have a detachment in Regina or Calgary any more than in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At Regina we have 192 men. Regina is the capital of the province, and a trading post for ail the forts. Recruits are brought to Regina and there drilled and prepared for their work. At Calgary we have some 49 men. Ail these men are not kept in the city of Calgary, but are distributed throughout the district. In the Calgary division there is a certain number of detachments, and the men are distributed throughout the division. We have so many men at Calgary, and so many men at Regina, but these do not cover only each city but the whole radius.

Every one realizes the necessity for this force, and 1 am not prepared to say that the necessity for it has decreased, or that the force should be decreased, or that it should not be increased. But I would like to know on what principle the government acts m maintaining or not maintaining it in any particular district. Take the district between Regina and the American boundary. You have population pouring in there, the country becoming pretty thickly settled, under what conditions do you take your force away from there and transfer it to some more remote district, less thickly populated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The divisions were made long ago. Take the country between Regina and the American boundary, we have a division at Lethbridge, another at Macleod, and another at Calgary. At each of these places we have barracks. We may decrease or increase the number

On what principle do you act in determining that the ordinary civil authorities shall be responsible for the prevention and detection of crime on the one hand, or that the Northwest Mounted Police shall be responsible on the other hand. For instance, about a year ago the posse comitatus of various counties in Ontario or Quebec was employed in chasing half a dozen criminals who roamed through the woods, and finally some of them were captured. It would be very convenient if we had a force of the mounted police to do this, but here it is done by the ordinary civil authorities. How do you get at the proper responsibility when you consider undertaking a duty of that kind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When the western provinces were organized we made an agreement with them under which each province pays us $75,000 a year, and we look after the administration of justice. We are at their service, and the Attorney General commands the services of the police when needed. -

The mounted police had in the first instance an authority or initiative. They did not wait for the warrant from the ordinary civil authority, but the inspectors issued warrants and the men served them. Is that initiative still retained?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. When the police were organized the officers were all justices of the peace, and also some of the non-commissioned officers, and they were continued in that capacity by the provincial government, so that there was no conflict.
If each province paid in proportion to the number of men in it, it would pay a much larger sum than $75,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is quite possible.

Is it a fact that the Northwest Mounted Police officers do the ordinary police work of the city where located? Take Caig-ary the city to which the Prime Minister has just referred. I am informed that in that city the Northwest

Mounted Police do the ordinary patrol duty of the city.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that at the present time Calgary and Regina have their own city police.
They have some, but it is said that the Northwest Mounted Police perform that duty as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that Calgary and Regina have their own police who look after city ordinances. But in case of a crime against the common law, the services of the Northwest Mounted Police may be still required. We are still bound, under our agreement, to act when asked by the Attorney General of the province.
Was the arrangement with the provinces made for any considerable time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For five years.
From what date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We had an arrangement for five years, and we renewed it last year.

I would like to substantiate what the Prime Minister has said with regard to the policing of the city Regina. True, the headquarters of the Mounted Police are located within the town limits of the city of Regina, and usually a large number of policemen are stationed there. I think that there is also a small Mounted Police station maintained there that is absolutely separate from the police organization of the city and maintained for Mounted Police purposes alone. We have our own police organization headed by the chief and with constables under him. I cannot make it too plain that the two organizations are separate and distinct. I had not intended to take part in this discussion, but while I am on my feet I desire to say a word further. Representations have been made to me with regard to the Pay given to the constables of the Northwest Mounted Police. I do not speak of the pay given to the officers, but in my opinion the pay given to the constables is not sufficient to induce the best men to go into the Mounted Police, and remain as policemen. We, who come from western Canada know that the cost of living is higher than in the east. I put some question on the Order Paper with respect to the pay of the Mounted Police, and I find that of the constables^ is from 60 cents to $1 per diem, and a living allowance estimated by the department to be worth $335 per annum. The department estimates the pay of the constables as beginning at $554 and increasing to $700 in the course of five years. That pay is not as much as the Mr. PORTER.
ordinary constable is given in the ordinary towns in the province of Saskatchewan, and not by any means as much as the ordinary constable obtains in the city of Regina. I asked if any difficulty had been experienced in the obtaining of recruits, and the reply was that no difficulty is experienced, but the rate of wages in the west induces a number of the best men to purchase their discharge. The reason is that they can obtain better positions by acting as constables in the various towns. It may be a good thing for the Northwest Mounted Police to educate constables for the towns of the west, but unless we give additional pay, as things are, I fear we cannot obtain the best men for the Mounted Police force.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Up to the present time, we have had no difficulty in getting the number of men required, and it is, I believe, the universal testimony that the force is a high class one, and that the quality of the men could not be better. The men start on 60 cents a day and increase gradually until they reach an average sum, with allowance, of $700 a year. My hon. friend (Mr. Martin, Regina) must remember also that when a man has served O'.) vears in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police he is entitled to a pension. I know of some men who started early in life who served 20 years, and, when a little over 40 had a pension,-which, of course, they had well earned, and which the country did not grudge. I think that, on the whole, with the pay, the allowance, and the pension in addition we have been able to keep the force on a very high footing, indeed. We are exposed to lose men, and we do lose some men, because of the attractions offered to young and vigorous men in the west in business, or farming, or other occupations. But I think the pay is reasonable.

What is the practice of the department in regard to obtaining supplies? For instance, at the headquarters at Regina a large amount of clothing and provisions must be provided. What is the practice of the department in regard to the matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All supplies are obtained by tender and the order is given to the lowest competitor. This applies to all except 25 per cent; there is a certain amount of small items which, as my hon. friend (Mr. Lake) knows, could not be obtained by tender.
It is now 11.30, and time to adjourn.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Oh, no. We
are just on the eve of working.
I did not understand that the hon. gentleman wanted much work done. I thought he wanted in bulk-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But I do not want to lose my time. There are items I want to put through.
I thought the arrangement was to give a certain amount in bulk-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We shall get a certain amount of bulk, I hope. But surely we are not to lose time?
There is lots of other work to go on with, to clear the Order Paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I hope to do that, but we cannot do it if we stop at 11.30.

The difficulty is that we do not get very good notice of the work that is coming up. On Friday night we were told that Bills were to be taken up, and after that, railway estimates. Later we were told that militia estimates were to be taken up. Finally, the Prime Minister takes up his own estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, the militia estimates were taken up on Friday night. Wo said that Bills would be taken up in the afternoon and Supply afterwards. We should have gone on with the estimates of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), but that hon. gentleman being confined to his house, I thought that, as I shall be leaving for Great Britain, I would ask my hon. friend to take up my estimates.

After the House rose on Friday night, I was speaking to the Minister of Agriculture, and he mentioned an item of the Minister of Customs which had already been passed that day, and the Minister of Agriculture said he did not know that item had been passed. So he said: We will take up the estimates of. the Minister of Militia on Monday after we get through with Bills.
There are gentlemen here who are prepared to discuss militia, but some gentlemen who wish to discuss the North West Mounted Police are not here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Very well, there are some items for pensions on page 45 to which no one will take exception, and we will pass them and then rise.
What business will be taken up to-morrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Bills first, then Trade and Commerce, Customs and Excise.
Some resolutions reported.
